steps: Start setting up your GmbH now. It usually takes 6 to 12 weeks in Germany.
Use employer of record for your first hires until month 4, so you can hire straight away.
Move your team onto your own company in month 4.
flags: In Germany an employer of record must hold a labour leasing licence, and the same person can usually be placed with you for at most 18 months. Your plan keeps people in the country beyond month 18, so this counts as a risk.
People who work only for you, full-time and under your direction, are usually treated as employees. Using contractors for them is risky, so employer of record or your own company is the safer choice.
Running a company where you do not work in the local language costs more, so the running cost has been raised by 30%.

review.summary: The recommended route is to set up your own German company (GmbH), starting setup in month 1 and moving the team onto it in month 4, with an employer of record covering the first hires until then. Over the plan period this costs 77,770 EUR on top of pay, against 138,020 EUR for staying on an employer of record, a difference of 60,250 EUR.
review.driver: All three checks (financial, risk and strategic) point towards your own company, giving a score of 3. The own-company route becomes cheaper than staying on an employer of record from month 5, when headcount reaches 6, and the team is planned to grow to 20 by month 24.
risks: Setup must be ready by month 4, and the flags note that a German GmbH usually takes 6 to 12 weeks, so any delay would extend reliance on the employer of record.

An employer of record can usually place the same person for at most 18 months, so keeping people on that route beyond month 18 would be a regulatory risk. The plan avoids this by moving everyone in month 4, but any slip changes that.
Using contractors for people who work only for you, full-time and under your direction is risky, as they are usually treated as employees.
